**Final PSD3 and PSR compromise texts signal the shape of Europe's next payments regime**

*Publication of the final compromise texts for PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation gives the industry its clearest view yet of the rules that will replace PSD2, with material changes to open banking access, fraud liability and national implementation.*

Two legal analyses published this week – from A&O Shearman and Lexology – examine the final compromise texts now circulating ahead of formal adoption. The split structure, a directly applicable regulation (PSR) paired with a directive (PSD3), is designed to close the implementation gaps that fragmented PSD2 across member states. The PSR will standardise payment execution, fraud prevention and open banking access rules without requiring national transposition, while PSD3 handles licensing and supervision.

For banks and payment institutions, the practical implications are substantial. The PSR tightens fraud liability frameworks and refines the conditions under which third-party providers can access payment accounts, moving beyond the screen-scraping ambiguities that dogged PSD2. A Finextra analysis argues the package demands more than compliance – it requires banks to rethink how they deliver payment services, particularly around data sharing and customer authentication.

The texts are expected to be formally adopted in the coming months, with an implementation timeline that will give firms a transition window. But the direction is now set: more harmonisation, stronger consumer protections and a broader open banking framework that edges toward open finance.

*Editorial note: The publication of final compromise texts is the most consequential regulatory development in today's feed, giving European payments firms the definitive basis for implementation planning.*

*Sources: [Final compromise texts for proposed Payment Services Package published](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/final-compromise-texts-for-proposed-2841425/) — A&O Shearman via JD Supra | [PSD3 and PSR published: what's changing for EU payment services?](https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=9ac8b1b8-7feb-4b88-8de3-1e7c6ebee46f) — Lexology | [When compliance is not enough: PSR and PSD3 demand a new mindset from banks](https://www.finextra.com/the-long-read/1648/when-compliance-is-not-enough-psr-and-psd3-demand-a-new-mindset-from-banks) — Finextra*

**UK government confirms design for streamlined payments regulation**

*The UK has set out core design decisions for consolidating payments oversight, a restructuring that will reshape how payment firms are supervised after the Payment Systems Regulator's absorption into the FCA.*

A legal briefing from Slaughter and May, published via JD Supra, analyses the UK government's confirmed approach to rationalising its payments regulatory architecture. The changes follow the decision to fold the Payment Systems Regulator into the Financial Conduct Authority, and the government has now confirmed the core design principles that will govern the new structure.

The consolidation matters because it will change reporting lines, supervisory expectations and potentially the enforcement posture that payment firms face. For firms operating across both the UK and EU, the timing is notable: the UK is simplifying its regulatory architecture just as the EU is finalising PSD3/PSR, creating two distinct but parallel reform programmes that will need to be navigated simultaneously. Firms with cross-border operations will need to track divergences carefully as both regimes take shape.

*Editorial note: Selected because the UK regulatory redesign runs in parallel with PSD3/PSR, and firms operating in both jurisdictions need to understand both tracks.*

*Sources: [Payments: UK government confirms core design decisions for new 'streamlined' regulatory framework](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/payments-uk-government-confirms-core-7424127/) — Slaughter and May via JD Supra*

**Nexi brings Wero to German e-commerce, testing account-to-account payments at checkout**

*Nexi's launch of Wero for online payments in Germany marks the first major acquirer integration of the EPI-backed scheme in e-commerce, a practical test of whether account-to-account payments can gain traction at the point of sale.*

Nexi has begun offering Wero as a payment method for German e-commerce merchants, making it one of the first large acquirers to integrate the European Payments Initiative's account-to-account scheme into online checkout. The move takes Wero beyond peer-to-peer transfers – where it launched – and into the merchant payments space where it will compete directly with cards and established wallets.

The significance lies in distribution. Wero's viability as an alternative to card networks depends on whether acquirers and payment service providers build it into their merchant offerings. Nexi, as one of Europe's largest payment processors, provides meaningful scale in the German market. But the real test is consumer adoption at checkout, where card-on-file habits and established wallet preferences create substantial inertia. Germany's relatively high share of bank-transfer-based payments may make it more receptive territory than other European markets.

This is a story to watch rather than celebrate. Account-to-account payment schemes have struggled to convert merchant acceptance into consumer usage elsewhere. Wero's progress in German e-commerce over the next twelve months will be a credible indicator of whether EPI can deliver on its ambitions.

*Editorial note: Wero's move into e-commerce via a major acquirer is a material step for the EPI scheme, and Germany is a strategically important test market.*

*Sources: [Nexi launches Wero for eCommerce in Germany](https://ibsintelligence.com/ibsi-news/nexi-launches-wero-for-ecommerce-in-germany/) — IBS Intelligence*

**US real-time payments accelerate, narrowing the gap with European and Asian markets**

*Growth in US real-time payment volumes is reaching an inflection point, with implications for European processors and fintechs operating transatlantically.*

PYMNTS reports that US real-time payments are entering a high-growth phase as use cases expand beyond early adopter segments. The US has long lagged markets such as the UK, India and Brazil in instant payment adoption, but the combination of FedNow's maturing network and RTP's expanding reach is driving volume growth across bill pay, payroll and business-to-business use cases.

For European payments firms, this matters in two ways. First, transatlantic payment corridors will increasingly need to accommodate real-time expectations on both ends, raising the bar for cross-border infrastructure. Second, the strategic assumptions that European instant payment schemes such as SEPA Instant and Wero are built on – that real-time is the default – are now being validated by the US market's trajectory, reinforcing the case for continued investment. The convergence also creates opportunities for European fintechs and processors with instant payment expertise to compete for US market share.

*Editorial note: US real-time payment growth is relevant context for European firms with transatlantic operations and validates strategic bets on instant payments infrastructure.*

*Sources: [US Real-Time Payments Hit High-Growth Phase as Use Cases Multiply](https://www.pymnts.com/real-time-payments/2026/us-real-time-payments-hit-high-growth-phase-as-use-cases-multiply/) — PYMNTS*
